1 About these cookbooks

Each “GUESS for X” cookbook is a set of short recipes for one field. This one, the Kitchen, holds what they all share. The field books link back here instead of repeating it.

Every recipe has the same parts:

  • You have / you want: the situation and the goal, so you can tell quickly whether the recipe is the one you need.
  • Ingredients: the data and commands it uses.
  • Steps: code to type into the GUESS console (or paste, then Shift+Enter). Each recipe starts from scratch and loads its own data.
  • How it works: what the commands did, and what the result means.
  • Variations and pitfalls: related tasks, and where the method misleads.

Recipes are tagged Basic, Intermediate or Advanced. The data files named in the steps are in the cookbooks’ data folder. Open them with File → Open (or drag them onto the page) and GUESS keeps a copy, so makeFromGDF("karate.gdf") finds it afterwards. sample.gdf is the graph GUESS opens with.

Every code sample in these books is run by the build, so if a recipe doesn’t work as printed, that’s a bug: please report it.

2 Getting data in

2.1 Open a network file Basic

You have a network saved by another tool. You want it in GUESS.

Ingredients: karate.gdf · makeFromGDF and friends

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")

How it works. Each format has its own loader. All of them replace the current graph, turn the file’s attributes into fields, and keep the file’s positions if it has them:

format command
GDF (GUESS, GUESS 2006) makeFromGDF
GraphML (yEd, Cytoscape, networkx) makeFromGraphML
GEXF (Gephi) makeFromGEXF
GML makeFromGML
DOT (Graphviz) makeFromDOT
Pajek .net makeFromPajek
UCINET DL makeFromDL
CSV / TSV makeFromCSV (next recipe)
Excel .xlsx makeFromExcel
Cytoscape: SIF, Cytoscape.js JSON, CX / CX2, XGMML, session .cys, nested networks makeFromSIF, makeFromCYJS, makeFromCX, makeFromXGMML, makeFromCYS, makeFromNNF
Biology: PSI-MI TAB and XML, SBML, BioPAX, KEGG, WikiPathways makeFromMITAB, makeFromPSIMI, makeFromSBML, makeFromBioPAX, makeFromKGML, makeFromGPML
RDF (Turtle, N-Triples, RDF/XML) makeFromRDF

makeFromFile picks the loader for you: from the extension, or from the content when the extension doesn’t say (.xml, .txt, .json), and File → Open and dropping a file use it. In a script, makeFromURL("https://…/graph.gexf") downloads and opens a file in one step. exportCYJS("g.cyjs") writes a file Cytoscape opens.

Variations. makeSample() lists the classic networks GUESS has built in (the karate club, Les Misérables, Florentine families, Davis’s southern women…). makeSample("karate") opens one without a file.

2.2 Build a network from a spreadsheet Basic

You have a table of who is linked to whom. You want a network.

Ingredients: friends.csv (columns Source, Target, Weight) · makeFromCSV

makeFromCSV("friends.csv")
getEdgeSchema()

How it works. A CSV whose first two columns are named Source and Target (as Gephi expects) is read as an edge table: one row per edge, and every other column becomes an edge field (weight here). A first row of node names and a first column of the same names is read as an adjacency matrix instead. Edges are undirected unless the table has a Type column saying Directed, or you pass directed=true.

Pitfalls. Spreadsheets often list a tie once in each direction, or repeat it per contact. Here, ana,ben appears three times. See Merge duplicate edges into weights.

2.3 Add attributes from a second table Basic

You have a network, plus a spreadsheet of facts about the nodes (age, team, gene expression…). You want those facts as node fields.

Ingredients: friends.csv · friends-nodes.csv (columns Id, team, age)

makeFromCSV("friends.csv")
makeFromCSV("friends-nodes.csv")
ana.team, ana.age

How it works. Opening a CSV with an Id column but no Source/Target doesn’t replace the graph. It adds the columns to the nodes whose names match the Id, and creates nodes for Ids that aren’t in the network yet (ivy, who has no ties). Numbers become numeric fields, so age > 30 works straight away.

Variations. makeFromCSV("edges.csv", "nodes.csv") reads both tables at once.

2.4 Bring in a networkx or igraph graph Intermediate

You have a graph built in Python, or want an algorithm GUESS doesn’t have. You want to move between GUESS and networkx.

Ingredients: toNetworkX · fromNetworkX · setField

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
import networkx as nx
G = toNetworkX()
setField(nx.load_centrality(G), "load")
sortBy(load)[-3:]

How it works. toNetworkX() hands you the current graph with every field as an attribute. setField(result, "name") stores what a networkx function returns: a dict of node values becomes a node field, a dict of node pairs becomes an edge field, and a list of node sets (communities) becomes a field holding each node’s group number. fromNetworkX(G) goes the other way and replaces the graph.

3 Cleaning

3.1 Merge duplicate edges into weights Basic

You have the same tie listed many times. You want one edge per pair, weighted by how often (or how much) it occurred.

Ingredients: friends.csv · simplify

makeFromCSV("friends.csv")
simplify()
(ana <-> ben).weight

How it works. simplify() merges edges joining the same two nodes (in the same direction, for directed edges) and adds up their weights. It also removes self-loops (fay to fay). combine="max", "mean", "min" or "first" combine weights differently. It’s one undo step.

3.2 Drop isolates and keep the main component Basic

You have a network with stray nodes and small fragments. You want to analyse the connected core.

Ingredients: friends.csv, friends-nodes.csv · giantComponent · removeDisconnected

makeFromCSV("friends.csv"); makeFromCSV("friends-nodes.csv"); simplify()
removeDisconnected()                # ivy, who has no ties
showOnly(giantComponent())          # hide gus and hal's pair

How it works. removeDisconnected() deletes nodes with no edges and returns them. giantComponent() is the largest connected piece. showOnly hides the rest without deleting it (showAll() brings it back), while remove(g.nodes - giantComponent()) deletes it.

Pitfalls. Measures like closeness and average path length are only meaningful within a component. Decide whether fragments are noise or findings before you drop them.

3.3 Make, rename and fill fields Basic

You have values to store or derive. You want them as fields you can query, colour and size by.

makeFromGDF("sample.gdf")
addNodeField("senior", BOOLEAN, false)
(dept == "dept4").senior = true
addEdgeField("heavy", BOOLEAN, false)
(freq > 50).heavy = true
getNodeSchema()

How it works. addNodeField(name, type, default) and addEdgeField create a field with a default value. Assigning to a set ((… ).senior = true) sets it on every member. The types are VARCHAR (text), INTEGER, DOUBLE, BOOLEAN. Python works too: for n in g.nodes: n.senior = n.degree > 5.

Pitfalls. Field, node and colour names are reserved, so they can’t be used as variable names. x = 5 is an error because x is the field holding each node’s position, and so are size, color, label and your own fields’ names. Pick another name (xs = …).

4 Asking questions

4.1 Select by value Basic

You have a field. You want the nodes or edges that match.

makeFromGDF("sample.gdf")
dept4 = (dept == "dept4")
busy = (freq > 100)
dept.find("dept9")                 # the same as dept == "dept9"
(dept like "dept1%")               # SQL patterns: % any run, _ one character
len(dept4), len(busy)

How it works. In GUESS, comparing a field with a value doesn’t give True/False; it gives the set of matching elements. Sets can be coloured, hidden, counted or passed to any command. field.find(value) is a plain-method spelling of field == value.

4.2 Combine and subtract sets Basic

makeFromGDF("sample.gdf")
a = (dept == "dept4")
b = (degree > 5)
(a & b).color = red                 # in dept4 and well connected
(a | b).size = 20                   # either
a.difference(b).color = orange      # in dept4 but not well connected

How it works. & is intersection and | union, and .difference() removes members. They work on any GUESS sets, including edges. Assigning a field on a set assigns it on every member.

Pitfalls. Between sets of nodes, - doesn’t subtract: a - b is the edges joining a and b (see the next recipe). Use .difference().

4.3 Find the edges between groups Basic

You want the ties linking two sets of nodes, or the ties of one node.

makeFromGDF("sample.gdf")
a = (dept == "dept4"); b = (dept == "dept9")
(a <-> b).color = red               # edges between the two departments (also a - b)
(v1 -> g.nodes).width = 4            # v1's outgoing edges
interEdges(dept).color = gray        # every edge that crosses departments

How it works. ->, <- and <-> between nodes or sets give the edges in that direction (<-> either way). interEdges(field) and intraEdges(field) give the edges that cross between values of a field or stay within one.

4.4 Rank and group Basic

makeFromGDF("sample.gdf")
sortBy(betweenness)[-5:]                    # the top five
[(grp[0].dept, len(grp)) for grp in groupBy(dept)]
dept.distinct                               # every value once
table(dept == "dept4")                      # look at them in the data table

How it works. sortBy(field) sorts ascending, so the largest values are at the end. groupBy(field) returns one set per value, and groupAndSortBy orders the groups by size. table(seq) opens the data table on just those rows, where you can sort columns and edit values.

5 Measuring

5.1 Size, density and the usual summary Basic

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
graphStats()

How it works. graphStats() prints the measures most papers report: nodes, edges, density, mean degree, components, diameter, average path length, average clustering, transitivity and degree assortativity (plus reciprocity for directed graphs). Each is also a command on its own (density(), diameter(), transitivity()…).

5.2 Who is central? Basic

You want to find the important nodes, and to know which kind of important you mean.

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
frLayout()
sizeBy(betweenness, 8, 40)
colorBy(closeness, yellow, red)
labelBy(label)

How it works. These centrality fields are computed the first time you use them:

field high when a node…
degree, indegree, outdegree has many ties
strength has heavy ties (sum of weights)
betweenness lies on many shortest paths: a broker or gatekeeper
closeness, harmonic is few steps from everyone (harmonic copes with fragments)
eigenvector is tied to nodes that are themselves well tied
pagerank is pointed to by important nodes (directed)
hub, authority points to good authorities / is pointed to by good hubs
constraint, effsize spans structural holes (Burt): low constraint = broker
coreness sits in a deep k-core

Pitfalls. Centralities disagree, and the disagreement is informative: a node with low degree but high betweenness is a bridge between groups. Don’t report “the most central” node without saying which measure.

5.3 Look at distributions Basic

makeFromGDF("lesmis.gdf")
plotHistogram(degree)
plotDistrib(betweenness)

How it works. plotHistogram(field) counts values in bins. plotDistrib(field) plots each node’s value in rank order, which makes heavy tails (a few hubs, many small nodes) obvious. The charts appear in a panel and can be saved as images.

5.4 Scatter two measures Basic

You want to see how two measures go together: are the best-connected characters also the ones on most shortest paths?

makeFromGDF("lesmis.gdf")
plotScatter(degree, betweenness)                            # one dot per node
plotScatter(degree, ends=true, line=[(1, 1), (36, 36)])     # degree at both ends of every edge

How it works. plotScatter(x, y) draws one dot per node (or edge, for edge fields) in the element’s own colour. Pointing at a dot highlights its node in the graph, and clicking selects it, so the outliers are a click away: here, characters with modest degree but high betweenness are the brokers between parts of the story. plotScatter(field, ends=true) plots the value at one end of every edge against the other end (both ways round for undirected edges). Dots near the diagonal mean like links to like, which is what assortativity(field) measures. line= adds a dashed reference line, log=true (or logX=, logY=) uses log axes, and xrange=/yrange= fix the axes.

Pitfalls. Many dots on top of each other look like one: use log axes for heavy-tailed measures, or colour the nodes first (colorize(...)) so the dots carry a third variable.

5.5 Fit a power law Intermediate

You want to know whether a degree distribution has a power-law tail, p(k) ∝ k^−α, and what α is.

makeFromGDF("polblogs-sample.gdf")
plotFrequency(degree, cumulative=true, log=true, fit=true)
fitPowerLaw(degree)                       # {'alpha': ..., 'sigma': ..., 'kmin': ..., 'n': ..., 'ks': ...}
import csv
rows = list(csv.DictReader(open("degree-sequences.csv")))
internet = [int(r["degree"]) for r in rows if r["network"].startswith("Internet")
            for _ in range(int(r["count"]))]
fitPowerLaw(internet)                     # the whole 2006 Internet: alpha about 2.08, from k = 5

How it works. plotFrequency(field, cumulative=true, log=true) plots the share of nodes with at least each degree, which is much less noisy in the tail than a histogram. fit=true adds the fitted power law as a dashed line. fitPowerLaw estimates α by maximum likelihood (not by drawing a line through the log-log plot, which is biased) and gives its standard error sigma. Unless you pass kmin=, it chooses where the tail starts by the Kolmogorov–Smirnov method; n is how many values the fit used. It also takes a plain list of numbers, as for the Internet’s 22,963 degrees in degree-sequences.csv, a network too big to draw.

Pitfalls.

  • A tail of a few dozen nodes can’t establish a power law: look at n and sigma before quoting α.
  • A small KS distance doesn’t rule out other heavy tails, such as an exponential or log-normal one; compare them before claiming a power law.
  • Some growth models give a power law in k + a rather than k (Price’s model, for one). fitPowerLaw(degree, shift=a) fits that form; fitting k directly then reads too low.

5.6 Charts of your own with Altair Intermediate

You want a chart GUESS has no command for, such as one measure plotted against another, and you want it linked to the graph like the built-in charts.

Ingredients: lesmis.gdf · nodeData · Altair (alt)

makeFromGDF("lesmis.gdf")
louvainClusters();
alt.Chart(nodeData("degree", "betweenness", "louvain_class")).mark_circle(size=60).encode(
    x="degree", y="betweenness", color="louvain_class:N", tooltip="name")
alt.Chart(nodeData("louvain_class")).mark_bar().encode(
    x="louvain_class:N", y="count()")

How it works. nodeData(...) gives one row per character with the fields you name, and Altair turns rows into any chart. A cell whose value is a chart shows it in the dock. alt is imported the first time you use it. GUESS knows degree is a number and louvain_class a field, so plain x="degree" works; the :N asks for the community numbers to be treated as categories. Valjean stands far above everyone in the scatter: betweenness 1624 with 36 contacts. Each row carries its character’s id, so pointing at a dot highlights that character in the graph and clicking selects them. A bar stands for the query it counts (louvain_class == 2): pointing at it lights up the whole community, and clicking selects it.

Variations. Add .add_params(alt.selection_interval()) to the scatter and drag a box over it: the characters inside are selected, and sel holds them. Click ● Live on a chart and it redraws after every change. Run louvainClusters(); again and the bar chart follows. nodeData(dept == "x", ...) charts just some nodes, and edgeData("weight") gives one row per edge.

5.7 Read the adjacency matrix Intermediate

You want the network as a matrix, with groups as blocks.

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
louvainClusters()
showMatrix(order=louvain_class)
makeFromGDF("southern-women.gdf")
showMatrix(rows=(kind == "event"), cols=(kind == "woman"), numbers=true)

How it works. showMatrix() draws a row and a column per node and a dark cell for each edge. order=field sorts the rows and columns by a field, with lines between its groups, so communities show as dense blocks on the diagonal. weight= shades cells by an edge field, and numbers=true writes each cell’s value (for small matrices). rows= and cols= give a rectangular matrix, such as the incidence matrix of people and the events they attended. Pointing at a cell highlights its edge and two nodes.

Pitfalls. Without an order the matrix looks like noise even when the network has strong groups: the blocks only appear once rows are sorted by something meaningful. Above a few hundred nodes, cells shrink below a pixel.

5.8 Paths and distances Basic

makeFromGDF("lesmis.gdf")
p = shortestPath(Napoleon, Javert)
p.color = red
heatMap(Valjean)                       # colour everyone by hops from Valjean
averagePathLength(), diameter()

How it works. shortestPath(a, b) returns the nodes and edges of one shortest path. weighted=true treats the edge weight as a length (so heavier means farther; invert weights first if they measure strength). heatMap(node) colours by distance and stores it in hops.

5.9 Coordinates for machine learning Advanced

You want to feed network position into a statistical model or a classifier, which needs numbers per node, not a graph.

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
embed(8, seed=1)
scatterLayout(emb0, emb1)
colorize(club)

How it works. embed(dims) gives each node coordinates (fields emb0, emb1…) such that nodes in similar network positions are close (node2vec). It takes many short random walks and factorises how often nodes appear near each other. scatterLayout(emb0, emb1) draws the first two coordinates. In the karate club the first coordinate alone separates the two sides fairly well (its correlation with club is about −0.6). The fields export with the rest of the data (exportCSV) for use in any modelling tool. p and q tune the walks: low q explores outwards (communities), low p stays local (roles).

6 Finding structure

6.1 Components, bridges and cut points Basic

makeFromGDF("sample.gdf")
colorize(component)
bridges().color = red                   # edges whose removal splits a part
cutNodes().size = 25                    # nodes whose removal splits a part

How it works. component numbers each connected piece (0 = largest). strongcomponent is the directed version. A bridge is the only link between two parts. A cut node holds two parts together. Both are where a network is fragile.

6.2 Cores and cliques Intermediate

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
colorBy(coreness, lightgray, red)
largestCliques()
showOnly(kCore(4))

How it works. The k-core is what remains after repeatedly removing nodes with fewer than k ties. coreness is the deepest core each node belongs to. A clique is a group in which everyone is tied to everyone. largestCliques() returns the biggest ones. Cores are robust and cliques are brittle (one missing tie breaks a clique), so prefer cores for noisy data.

6.3 Communities Basic

You want groups of nodes more tied to each other than to the rest.

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
frLayout()
leidenClusters()
colorize(leiden_class)
createConvexHull(leiden_class == 0, "255,200,200,90")
legendFor(leiden_class)

How it works. GUESS has many community methods. Each stores the result as a field (0 = the largest community):

command field good for
louvainClusters() louvain_class fast, standard (Gephi’s “Modularity”)
leidenClusters() leiden_class like Louvain, but every community is connected
infomapClusters() infomap_class directed flow: citations, web links
walktrapClusters(), fastGreedyClusters(), labelPropagationClusters(), … alternatives to compare
edgeBetweennessClusters(n) small graphs; a hierarchy you can cut

resolution= (Louvain, Leiden) above 1 gives more, smaller communities. modularity(field) scores any partition, including one you supply (modularity(dept)).

Hierarchical methods (walktrap, fast greedy) build a tree of merges. Draw it to choose how many communities to keep:

walktrapClusters()
showDendrogram(cut=4, paint=true)         # the tree, cut into 4 groups, nodes coloured to match

Pointing at a branch highlights its nodes; cut=k colours the k groups, paint=true gives the nodes the same colours, and field="name" stores the groups. cutDendrogram(k) re-cuts the stored field.

Pitfalls. Every method finds communities, even in random graphs. Check that the modularity is well above what you get after rewire(), and that the result is stable (seed=None, run again, then compareClusters).

6.4 Compare two groupings Intermediate

makeFromGDF("sample.gdf")
louvainClusters()
compareClusters(louvain_class, dept)               # 0 = unrelated, 1 = identical
compareClusters(louvain_class, dept, method="ari")
mixingMatrix(dept)

How it works. compareClusters gives normalized mutual information (or the adjusted Rand index) between two partitions, such as found communities and a known attribute. mixingMatrix(field) counts edges between each pair of values, which shows which groups mix.

To test a method where the right answer is known, run it on a benchmark network with planted communities:

makeLFR(250, mu=0.3, seed=1)              # 30% of each node's edges leave its community
louvainClusters()
compareClusters(louvain_class, community) # near 1 for small mu; falls as mu grows

makeLFR gives the planted groups in the field community. Every method finds them when mu is small and fails somewhere between about 0.3 and 0.5. Where it fails, and how gracefully, is the fair comparison between methods.

6.5 Compare with a random network Intermediate

You want to know whether a measure is surprising, or just what any network with the same degrees would give.

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
real = (averageClustering(), assortativity())
makeConfigurationModel(degree, simple=true)      # the same degrees, wired at random
wired = (averageClustering(), assortativity())
makeErdosRenyiRandom(34, 0.139)                  # only the same size and density
plain = averageClustering()
print(real, wired, plain)

How it works. A random network with the same degrees as the real one (the configuration model) is the usual baseline: whatever it shares with the real network comes from the degrees alone. The karate club’s clustering (0.57) is more than twice the rewired network’s (about 0.23): the club’s triangles are real structure, not an effect of its hubs. makeConfigurationModel(degree) copies the current graph’s degrees (any numeric field or list works); simple=true removes the self-loops and repeated edges the random wiring makes. makeExpectedDegree(weights) joins each pair independently with probability w_i w_j / Σw instead. makeErdosRenyiRandom(n, p) keeps only the size and density. rewire() does the same as the configuration model in place, by swapping edge ends.

Pitfalls.

  • One random network is one sample: repeat with different seeds and compare with the spread, not a single value.
  • Random generators are seeded (seed=0 by default), so the same call gives the same network every time. Pass seed=None for a new one each time, or other numbers for a set of samples.
  • The generators replace the current graph; save it first (saveState) or use a separate graph (newGraph).

6.6 Collapse groups into single nodes Intermediate

makeFromGDF("sample.gdf")
collapseBy(dept)

How it works. Each department becomes one meta-node, with edges summarising the ties between departments. expand(node) or expandAll() opens them again. Double-clicking a meta-node in the display does the same.

7 Laying out

7.1 Choose a layout Basic

makeFromGDF("lesmis.gdf")
forceAtlas2Layout()

How it works. No layout is “correct”. Choose by what you want to see:

you want try
clusters to separate forceAtlas2Layout(), frLayout(), sfdpLayout() (large graphs)
distances to mean graph distance kkLayout(), neatoLayout(), mdsLayout()
a hierarchy or flow, top to bottom dotLayout(), sugiyamaLayout(), dagLayout()
one node’s view of the world radialLayout(node), twopiLayout()
groups on a circle circleLayout(), circoLayout(), hiveLayout(field)
two kinds of node bipartiteLayout(field)
attributes as coordinates scatterLayout(x, y)

Layouts start from the current positions, so running one twice refines it. removeOverlap() (or noverlapLayout()) pushes overlapping nodes apart afterwards. For a hand-drawn look, lombardiLayout() draws edges as circular arcs that leave each node at evenly spread angles (a “Lombardi drawing”), and lombardiEdges() rounds the edges of any layout without moving the nodes:

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
lombardiLayout()                          # returns how even the angles were, before and after

Layouts are seeded, so the same network and starting positions give the same picture every time.

7.2 Pin nodes while the rest moves Basic

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
m1.x, m1.y = 100, 500
m34.x, m34.y = 900, 500
(m1, m34).fixed = true
frLayout()

How it works. Nodes with fixed = true stay put during layouts, and the others arrange themselves around them. Here the two rival leaders anchor the two ends of the picture. Dragging a node with the mouse also moves it.

8 Drawing

8.1 Colour, size and shape by data Basic

makeFromGDF("sample.gdf")
colorize(dept)                     # a distinct colour per value
sizeBy(degree, 6, 30)              # proportional to a number
shapeBy(jobfun)                    # a shape per value
sizeBy(freq, 1, 6)                 # edge widths, for an edge field
legendFor(dept)

How it works. colorize is for categories; colorBy(field, low, high) is a gradient for numbers. sizeBy(field, min, max) scales sizes (scale="log" or "sqrt" for skewed values). resizeLinear spaces sizes by rank. Legends follow the colours: re-run colorize and the legend updates.

directedEdges("arrow")       # arrowheads on directed edges
directedEdges("taper")       # back to the default: wide at the source, a point at the target
v1.strokewidth = 4           # a thicker outline marks one node

Directed edges are drawn tapered by default, with no arrowhead: in a user study (Holten and van Wijk, CHI 2009), tapered edges were read fastest and most accurately, and arrowheads among the worst. directedEdges("fade") uses a dark-to-light ramp instead. A node’s strokewidth field sets its outline (0 = the display’s default), which is a good way to mark a state without changing the fill. For a cyclic value, such as a phase or an angle, colorByPhase(field, period=) colours around a colour wheel so the two ends of the cycle match.

8.2 Labels that don’t collide Basic

makeFromGDF("lesmis.gdf")
forceAtlas2Layout()
sizeBy(degree, 5, 30)
g.nodes.labelvisible = true
g.nodes.labelpos = "outside"
optimizeLabels()
hideOverlappingLabels()

How it works. labelpos is where a node’s label goes: "right", "left", "above", "below", "inside" (fitted into the shape), or "outside", which lets GUESS choose a free spot. optimizeLabels() runs a longer search for positions, and hideOverlappingLabels() drops the labels that still collide, smallest nodes first. labelSizeBy(degree) makes important labels bigger. constantLabelSize(size=14) keeps labels the same size on screen as you zoom, so they stay readable on a big graph (zooming in then reveals more of them).

8.3 Outline groups and bundle the hairball Intermediate

makeFromGDF("lesmis.gdf")
forceAtlas2Layout()
louvainClusters(); colorize(louvain_class)
for grp in groupBy(louvain_class): createConvexHull(grp)
bundleEdges()

How it works. createConvexHull(set) shades the area around a set of nodes. bundleEdges() gathers edges that run in the same direction into bundles (MINGLE). method="fdeb" gives smoother curves, and passing a field (bundleEdges(louvain_class)) bundles within groups. removeBundles() undoes it.

8.4 Simplify a hairball with motifs Intermediate

makeFromGDF("sample.gdf")
findMotifs("fan", 3)
collapseMotifs("fan", 3)
len(g.nodes)

How it works. Big drawings are cluttered by small repeated shapes: fans (several leaves hanging off one node), connectors (nodes that all link to the same few others and nothing else) and cliques. findMotifs(kind, minimum) finds them, and collapseMotifs replaces each with a single meta-node labelled with its kind and size. Here the organisation’s 26 fans collapse, taking it from 402 nodes to 303 without losing anything: double-click a meta-node, or expandAll(), to open it.

8.5 Explore a crowded area with the lens Basic

Press L (or the Lens button in the toolbar) and move over a dense area: the lens lists the labels of everything under it, in a column beside the cursor, with lines to each node. The mouse wheel resizes it, Shift+wheel scrolls long lists, and a click pins it. excentricLens(true, radius=80) turns it on from the console.

9 Change over time

9.1 Save, compare and animate states Intermediate

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
frLayout()
ss("before")
remove(m1)                        # what if the instructor leaves?
colorize(component)
ss("after")
morph("before", 1500)

How it works. ss(name) saves the whole graph (membership, positions, every field) as a named state. ls(name) returns to it, and morph(name, ms) animates the change. Fields can be read in a state: betweenness["before"], m2["before"].color. States can be named with numbers (ss(1999)), which suits snapshots over time.

9.2 Show a network as of a date Intermediate

makeFromGDF("sample.gdf")
addEdgeField("since", INTEGER, 0)
for e in g.edges: e.since = e.freq          # pretend freq is a year
showTime(60, since)                         # edges that exist by "60"
showTime(150, since, window=50)             # only the last 50

How it works. showTime(t, field) shows only elements whose numeric field is at most t (and within window of it, if given). For elements that come and go, give them ranges with addRange(node, "1999-2003,2007") and use showTime(t). View → Timeline gives a slider.

To replay how a network grew, lay out the final network once and reveal it in arrival order, so every node appears where it will stay:

makePriceModel(200, c=2, a=1)             # a citation network; born = when each paper arrived
center(g.nodes)                           # frame the final picture
revealUpTo(20)                            # the first 20 papers and their citations
revealUpTo(199)                           # everything

revealUpTo(step) shows the nodes whose born field (or field=) is at most step, and the edges between them, and returns what arrived at exactly that step, ready to highlight. The growth models (makePriceModel, makeBarabasiAlbertRandom, makeGrowingNetwork, makeCopyingModel) set born themselves; for your own data, store the step or year in a field.

10 Sharing

10.1 Export a figure Basic

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
frLayout(); colorize(club)
exportSVG("karate.svg")
exportPDF("karate.pdf")
exportPNG("karate.png")

How it works. SVG and PDF are vector: the whole graph, at any size, with labels and legends, ready for a paper. PNG is the current view as you see it.

10.2 Tell a story with slides Intermediate

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
frLayout()
addSlide("The club before the split")
colorize(club)
addSlide("The two factions")
slides()

How it works. addSlide(note) saves the graph and the camera as a slide, and the Slides panel plays them, morphing from one to the next.

10.3 A one-page report Basic

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
louvainClusters()
report()
report("karate-report.html")

How it works. report() prints a summary of the graph: size, density, components, the degree distribution, path lengths, clustering, assortativity, the top nodes by degree, betweenness and PageRank, and any communities found so far. report("name.html") (or .md) saves it as a page to share. In the browser, it’s offered as a download.

10.4 A web page anyone can open Basic

You want to share an interactive network with people who don’t use GUESS.

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
louvainClusters(); colorize(louvain_class)
legendFor(louvain_class)
sizeBy(betweenness, 8, 30)
exportHTML("karate.html", title="The karate club")

How it works. exportHTML writes one self-contained page: the graph, its fields and legends, and a small viewer, with nothing to install and no connection needed. Readers can pan and zoom, search for a node, hover to read its fields and click to see its neighbours. It follows their light or dark setting. Email it, or put it on any web server. exportJSON("karate.json") writes the same graph for sigma.js and other web libraries.

Pitfalls. The page holds all the data fields. fields=false leaves them out when some shouldn’t travel.

10.5 Work with an AI assistant Basic

You want an assistant such as Claude to help explore a network, in your session, where you can see and undo what it does.

connectAssistant()

How it works. The assistant reaches GUESS through mcp/guess-mcp.mjs, a small bridge it starts itself once you add it to its MCP settings (see the manual, Working with an AI assistant). After connectAssistant(), ● assistant shows in the toolbar. The assistant can run Gython, read a summary of the graph and the command help, and look at the view. Everything it runs appears in the console as a cell marked assistant, so undo() and Edit → History… work on its steps as on yours. disconnectAssistant() ends it.

Pitfalls. The assistant’s service sees what its tools return, including screenshots and summaries of your data. Don’t connect it to data you couldn’t share with that service.

10.6 Save your work and your method Basic

makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
louvainClusters(); colorize(louvain_class)
saveSession("karate-analysis.guess")
history()

How it works. saveSession writes everything (graph, fields, states, view) to one file that makeFromSession (or File → Open) restores. history() lists the commands you ran, which is your method: save it as a .py file and execfile replays it on new data.

11 Capstone

11.1 Animate a process step by step Advanced

You want an app that runs a process on the network (here, an infection spreading from the best-connected member of the karate club) slowly enough to watch, with a live chart and a running commentary.

import random
makeFromGDF("karate.gdf")
frLayout()
constantLabelSize(size=14)
rnd = random.Random(4)
first = max(g.nodes, key=lambda n: n.degree)
run = {"sick": {first.name}, "new": [first], "curve": [(0, 1)]}

def look():
    for n in g.nodes:
        ill = n.name in run["sick"]
        n.color = "230,60,50" if ill else "120,160,220"
        n.width = n.height = 26 if n in run["new"] else (18 if ill else 12)
        n.strokewidth = 3 if n in run["new"] else 0          # the newest cases stand out
    fresh = {n.name for n in run["new"]}
    for e in g.edges:                                        # the edges the infection just crossed
        hit = (e.node1.name in fresh) != (e.node2.name in fresh) \
            and e.node1.name in run["sick"] and e.node2.name in run["sick"]
        e.color, e.width, e.linestyle = ("240,140,30", 3, "flow") if hit else ("160,160,160,120", 1, "solid")

def step():
    new = [m for n in g.nodes if n.name in run["sick"] for m in n.getNeighbors()
           if m.name not in run["sick"] and rnd.random() < 0.25]
    new = list({m.name: m for m in new}.values())
    run["sick"] |= {m.name for m in new}
    run["new"] = new
    run["curve"].append((len(run["curve"]), len(run["sick"])))
    look()
    return len(g.nodes) - len(run["sick"])                   # 0 stops the timer

def start():
    everyPaced(step, slow=0.9, fast=0.2)

def chart():
    t = len(run["curve"])
    return plotLine({"infected": run["curve"], "everyone": [(0, len(g.nodes)), (t, len(g.nodes))]},
                    title="Infected so far", xlabel="step", ylabel="people", yrange=(0, len(g.nodes)),
                    dashed=["everyone"], colors={"infected": "230,60,50", "everyone": "150,150,150"})

def story():
    names = " ".join(linkTo(n) for n in run["new"]) or "none"
    return (f"**{len(run['sick'])}** of {len(g.nodes)} infected. Newest: {names}. More in "
            "[the epidemics explainer](?app=explainers/networks/ch16-epidemics-on-networks/manifest.json).")

ui.layout(right=Column(Markdown(story), Chart(chart), Row(Button("Spread", onClick=lambda: start()))),
          sizes={"right": 360})
look()
for _ in range(3):
    step()

How it works.

  • Pacing. everyPaced(step, slow=, fast=) calls step on a timer that starts slow, speeds up, and slows down again as step’s return value (the steps left) runs out, so the start and end of a process can be watched and the middle doesn’t drag. Returning 0 or False stops it; steps= fixes the number of steps instead.
  • Making changes visible. The newest cases are bigger and outlined (strokewidth), and the edges the infection just crossed flow orange. A colour change alone is easy to miss on small nodes. constantLabelSize(size=14) keeps labels readable at any zoom.
  • Live text and charts. Markdown(story) and Chart(chart) take functions, which run again after every step. linkTo(n) writes a chip that highlights its node when pointed at and selects it when clicked. A Markdown link to ?app=…/manifest.json opens another app on the same site. In plotLine, dashed= and colors= mark a reference or theory curve and give it a matching colour.
  • Growth. For a network that grows, build the final network first, lay it out once, and give each node and edge the step it arrives in a born field. Then call revealUpTo(step) from the timer, so each node appears where it will stay.

Pitfalls. A process that runs at full speed is over before anyone sees it, which is what the pacing is for. Keep the work in step small: it runs inside the timer, and in the browser a slow step stalls the whole page. Do expensive simulations off screen and chart the results.

11.2 Capstone: an explorer for any network Advanced

The problem. You’ve just been handed a network file and want a quick, reusable way to look at it from every angle without typing a command for each view. This recipe builds a small explorer that works on any graph:

  • drop-downs to colour by any field and size by any numeric field;
  • a slider that hides weakly connected nodes;
  • buttons to find communities, lay out again and reset;
  • a click shows everything known about a node, and a right-click focuses on its neighbourhood;
  • the legend and status bar keep track of what’s shown.
makeFromGDF("sample.gdf")
fields = [f for f in getNodeSchema() if not f.builtin]          # the data's own fields
categories = [f.name for f in fields if len(f.distinct) <= 30]
numbers = [f.name for f in fields if all(isinstance(v, (int, float)) for v in f.values()) and len(f.distinct) > 1]
numbers = numbers + ["degree", "betweenness", "pagerank"]

def colour_by(name):
    if name in numbers and name not in categories:
        colorBy(name, lightgray, red)
    else:
        colorize(name)
    legendFor(name)
    StatusBar.setStatus(f"colour: {name}")

def size_by(name):
    sizeBy(name, 4, 30)

def min_degree(v):
    showOnly(degree >= int(v))
    shown.text = f"{len(degree >= int(v))} of {len(g.nodes)} nodes with degree >= {int(v)}"

def details(n):
    vals = ", ".join(f"{f.name}={getattr(n, f.name)}" for f in fields[:8])
    about.text = f"{n.name}: degree {n.degree}; {vals}"

def communities():
    louvainClusters()
    colour_by("louvain_class")

shown, about = Label(""), Label("click a node")
panel = Panel("Explore",
              Dropdown(categories + [n for n in numbers if n not in categories], label="colour", onChange=colour_by),
              Dropdown(numbers, label="size", onChange=size_by),
              Slider(0, 10, 0, label="minimum degree", onChange=min_degree),
              Button("Communities", onClick=communities),
              Button("Lay out", onClick=lambda: forceAtlas2Layout()),
              Button("Show all", onClick=lambda: (showAll(), min_degree(0))),
              shown, about, position="bottom")
ui.dock(panel)
graphevents.clickNode = details
item = NodeEditorPopup.addItem("Focus on neighbourhood")
item.menuEvent = lambda n: showOnly(egoNetwork(n, 2))
min_degree(0)
colour_by(max(categories, key=lambda c: len(getattr(Node, c).distinct)) if categories else "degree")
size_by("degree")
center()

How it works.

  • Reading the fields. getNodeSchema() lists the graph’s fields, and builtin marks GUESS’s own (position, colour, visibility). The recipe sorts the data’s fields into categories (few distinct values) and numbers, adds three computed measures, and offers them in two Dropdowns. Choosing one calls colorize or colorBy (with a live legend), or sizeBy, with the field’s name: every command that takes a field also takes its name as a string.
  • Filtering. The Slider calls showOnly(degree >= v), a query built from its value.
  • The rest. The buttons wrap commands from this book. graphevents and NodeEditorPopup add click and right-click behaviour. Because nothing in it names a field of the sample data, the explorer works unchanged on any file: replace the first line.
